07 – Why do our results differ from the authors’? (case study 2)

Testing the possible causes, one at a time

Author

Minh Le, Jeanne Leclerc

Published

October 7, 2026

Goal

Notebooks 05 and 06 left two differences with the authors:

  1. gene selection: our best protocol (B+, the wrapper’s defaults) recovered 160 of the authors’ 174 selected genes, missed 14 and added 7;
  2. orientations: on the rebuilt input, the links of the network were mostly recovered, but many orientations and genuine causations were not.

Here we test the possible causes one at a time, each with a small experiment.

Inputs: the MI tables and recovered counts of notebook 05 (results/case2/05_rebuild_input/), the network of notebook 06, the authors’ files, and one extra MIIC run on the authors’ input without its duplicated columns (results/case2/07_differences/authors_dedup/, made with scripts/run_miic.R, see section 5).

Setup

library(Seurat)
library(miic)

nb05_dir    <- file.path(root, "results", "case2", "05_rebuild_input")
nb06_dir    <- file.path(root, "results", "case2", "06_rebuilt_network")

                     col_names = c("ligand", "receptor"), show_col_types = FALSE)
row_type <- case_when(!is.na(mosaic$labels_Fibroblasts) ~ "Fibroblasts",
                      !is.na(mosaic$labels_T_cell)      ~ "T_cell",
                      !is.na(mosaic$labels_DCs)         ~ "DCs")
col_type <- column_cell_type(mosaic, row_type)

# The authors' selected genes per cell type (without L-R genes, metadata and suffixes), as in notebook 05
authors_selected <- map(set_names(cell_types), \(t) {
  genes <- unique(strip(names(mosaic)[col_type == t & !str_detect(names(mosaic), "^(labels|condition)_")]))
  setdiff(genes, lr_roles$gene[lr_roles$cell_type == t])
})

Part 1 – Gene selection

1. A different version of the code?

The authors’ server job ran on 21 January 2025. The CausalCCC functions (causalCCC.utils.R, causalCCC.wrapper.R) were added to the public repository miicTeam/CausalCCC on 6 December 2024, and the md5 checksums of both files are identical in all five later commits, up to 0aa8586 (23 January 2025), which only changes the README (checked with the GitHub API on 7 October 2026). And notebook 04 showed that miic itself gives exactly the authors’ network.

Unless the authors used unpublished code, the code version is not the cause.

2. A different gene order?

causalCCC.MIselection() computes MI in blocks of 100 genes, each block in one call to miic. If the result for a gene depended on the other genes of its block, a different gene order in the authors’ Seurat object would change the MI values. We recompute the MI of two features of interest in dendritic cells after shuffling the gene order, and compare with notebook 05.

order_file <- file.path(results_dir, "mi_shuffled_order.rds")

if (file.exists(order_file)) {
  mi_shuffled <- readRDS(order_file)
} else {
  MIselection <- causalCCC.MIselection   # with the Seurat 5 fix of notebook 05
  body(MIselection) <- parse(text = gsub('slot = "counts"', 'layer = "counts"',
                                         deparse(body(MIselection)), fixed = TRUE))[[1]]
  set.seed(1)
  shuffled <- sample(nrow(rebuilt$counts))
  so <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = rebuilt$counts[shuffled, ], meta.data = rebuilt$meta)
  invisible(capture.output(suppressMessages(
    mi_shuffled <- MIselection(so, interact_ident = "cell_type", oneinteract = "DCs", goi = c("CD74", "CXCR4"),
                               metadata_list = c("labels", "condition"), return_full = TRUE))))
  mi_shuffled <- as_tibble(mi_shuffled) |> mutate(foi = as.character(foi))
  saveRDS(mi_shuffled, order_file)
}

mi_shuffled |>
  filter(foi %in% c("CD74", "CXCR4")) |>
  inner_join(filter(mi_tables, cell_type == "DCs"), by = c("variables", "foi"), suffix = c("_shuffled", "_original")) |>
  summarise(pairs = n(), largest_difference = max(abs(value_shuffled - value_original)))
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  pairs largest_difference
  <int>              <dbl>
1 34660                  0

The values are exactly the same: each MI value depends only on the two variables. Since our counts are the authors’ counts (notebook 05, section 2), our MI values are the authors’. The differences can only come from the choices made when selecting genes from these values.

3. Different selection settings?

Three settings of the wrapper could have been changed:

  • the number of genes n_genes kept by causalCCC.MIselection() (default max(15, min(4 × genes of interest, 100)));
  • the cap of 8 ligands or receptors used as features of interest in each run (in the wrapper, ligands[1:min(length(ligands), 8)]);
  • the metadata used as features of interest, on the sender and receiver sides.

run_protocol() generalises protocol B of notebook 05 (one run per sender → receiver direction) to these settings, and score() counts the authors’ selected genes we miss and the genes we add.

directions <- lr_pairs |>
  transmute(sender = col_type[ligand], receiver = col_type[receptor],
            ligand = strip(ligand), receptor = strip(receptor))

mi_by_type <- split(mi_tables, mi_tables$cell_type)

run_protocol <- function(meta_sender, meta_receiver, cap = 8, n_genes = default_n_genes) {
  one_side <- function(t, goi, meta) {
    goi <- head(unique(goi), cap)
    select_genes(mi_by_type[[t]], foi = c(goi, meta), n_genes = n_genes(goi))
  }
  runs <- directions |>
    group_by(sender, receiver) |>
    summarise(sender_genes   = list(one_side(first(sender), ligand, meta_sender)),
              receiver_genes = list(one_side(first(receiver), receptor, meta_receiver)),
              .groups = "drop")
  map(set_names(cell_types), \(t) {
    unique(c(unlist(runs$sender_genes[runs$sender == t]), unlist(runs$receiver_genes[runs$receiver == t])))
  })
}

score <- function(selected, protocol) {
  map(cell_types, \(t) {
    ours <- setdiff(selected[[t]], c(lr_roles$gene[lr_roles$cell_type == t], "labels", "condition"))
    tibble(protocol, cell_type = t,
           missing = length(setdiff(authors_selected[[t]], ours)),
           extra   = length(setdiff(ours, authors_selected[[t]])))
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

both_metadata <- c("labels", "condition")

The number of genes. With both metadata on both sides and the cap of 8, we vary n_genes, either as the default formula or as a fixed number:

n_genes_tests <- c(list("default" = default_n_genes),
                   map(set_names(paste("fixed", c(20, 24, 25, 26, 30))),
                       \(name) { n <- as.integer(str_extract(name, "[0-9]+")); \(goi) n }))

imap(n_genes_tests, \(f, name) score(run_protocol(both_metadata, both_metadata, cap = 8, n_genes = f), name)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  group_by(protocol) |>
  # detail first: inside summarise(), a new column hides the column of the same name for the next ones
  summarise(detail = paste(cell_type, missing, extra, sep = ":", collapse = "  "),
            missing = sum(missing), extra = sum(extra))

With 25 genes per run, fibroblasts and T cells are reproduced exactly (0 missing, 0 extra). Below 25, genes are missing; above, genes are added. Only 5 dendritic cell genes are still missing.

The 5 missing dendritic cell genes. For each, its rank among all genes by MI with each feature of interest of dendritic cells (rank 1 = highest MI):

They are the top 3 genes of TMEM219 (PFDN5, VAMP8, GRN) and the top 2 of TNFRSF14 (ARL6IP5, NDUFS5), so the top-3 rule of causalCCC.MIselection() selects them as soon as these two receptors are features of interest. But the cap of 8 removes them: TMEM219 is the 10th receptor of the fibroblasts → dendritic cells direction and TNFRSF14 the 9th of the T cells → dendritic cells direction.

metadata_options <- list(none = NULL, labels = "labels", condition = "condition", both = both_metadata)

expand_grid(sender = names(metadata_options), receiver = names(metadata_options), cap = c(8, Inf)) |>

The authors’ selection is reproduced exactly (0 missing, 0 extra in all three cell types) by: one wrapper run per sender → receiver direction, all the ligands or receptors of the direction as features of interest (no cap of 8), the subtype metadata (labels) as a feature of interest on both sides, and 25 genes per run. Adding condition on one or both sides changes nothing.

Part 2 – Orientations

4. Same input, same network

Notebook 04 already ruled out the MIIC step itself: on the authors’ input, our run gives exactly their links, orientations and genuine causations. So differences in orientations can only come from the input.

5. The duplicated columns?

Part 1 shows that our rebuilt input would contain exactly the authors’ genes with the right settings. The authors’ input without its 14 duplicated columns is therefore the input we would build ourselves. We ran MIIC on it with the server’s settings (one thread, same seed), with scripts/run_miic.R:

dedup_dir <- file.path(results_dir, "authors_dedup")

# How the input was made: the authors' files minus every column identical to an earlier column of the same cell type
dropped <- unlist(map(cell_types, \(t) {
  block <- mosaic[row_type == t, col_type == t]
  names(block)[duplicated(as.list(block))]
}))
dropped

 [7] "S100A6_T_cell"       "SH3BGRL3_T_cell"     "H3F3B"              
[10] "ANXA2"               "S100A10_DCs"         "TMSB10_DCs"         
[13] "LGALS1_DCs"          "S100A4_DCs"         
dedup_result <- readRDS(file.path(dedup_dir, "miic_result.rds"))
lr_links_authors <- link_name(lr_pairs$ligand, lr_pairs$receptor)

edges_authors <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "edgesList.miic.summary.txt"), show_col_types = FALSE)
edges_dedup   <- as_tibble(dedup_result$all.edges.summary) |>
  filter(!(link_name(x, y) %in% lr_links_authors & Nxy_ai %in% 0))   # placeholder rows (notebook 02)
edges_ours    <- read_tsv(file.path(nb06_dir, "edges.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Every variable identified as "<gene>_<cell type>", so that the three networks can be compared;
# the two copies of a duplicated gene become one node
key_of <- tibble(variable = names(mosaic), cell_type = col_type) |>
  mutate(key = if_else(str_detect(variable, "^(labels|condition)_"), variable,
                       paste0(strip(variable), "_", cell_type))) |>
  pull(key, name = variable)
key_of_ours <- set_names(unique(c(edges_ours$x, edges_ours$y)))

gene_links <- function(edge_list, keys) {
  edge_list |>
    filter(type == "P") |>
    mutate(a = keys[x], b = keys[y]) |>
    filter(a != b, !link_name(x, y) %in% c(lr_links_authors, link_name(keys[lr_pairs$ligand], keys[lr_pairs$receptor]))) |>
    transmute(link = link_name(a, b),
              orientation = if_else(a == pmin(a, b) | infOrt %in% c(1, 6), infOrt, -infOrt),
              is_causal) |>
    distinct(link, .keep_all = TRUE)
}

networks <- list(authors = gene_links(edges_authors, key_of),
                 authors_without_duplicates = gene_links(edges_dedup, key_of),
                 ours_notebook_06 = gene_links(edges_ours, key_of_ours))

map(networks, \(n) tibble(links = nrow(n), oriented = sum(abs(n$orientation) == 2),
                          bidirected = sum(n$orientation == 6), genuine_causation = sum(n$is_causal == "Y"))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "network")

Pairwise comparison. For two networks: the Jaccard index of their gene–gene links, and, on the shared links, the fraction with the same orientation and the number of genuine causations found in both.

compare_networks <- function(a, b) {
  shared <- inner_join(networks[[a]], networks[[b]], by = "link", suffix = c("_a", "_b"))
  tibble(comparison = paste(a, "vs", b),
         jaccard = nrow(shared) / n_distinct(c(networks[[a]]$link, networks[[b]]$link)),
         shared_links = nrow(shared),
         same_orientation = mean(shared$orientation_a == shared$orientation_b),
         opposite_orientation = sum(abs(shared$orientation_a) == 2 & shared$orientation_a == -shared$orientation_b),
         causal_a = sum(shared$is_causal_a == "Y"), causal_b = sum(shared$is_causal_b == "Y"),
         causal_both = sum(shared$is_causal_a == "Y" & shared$is_causal_b == "Y"))
}

bind_rows(compare_networks("authors", "authors_without_duplicates"),
          compare_networks("authors_without_duplicates", "ours_notebook_06"),
          compare_networks("authors", "ours_notebook_06")) |>
  print(width = Inf)

centres         <- c("CXCL12_Fibroblasts", "CXCR4_DCs", "CXCR4_T_cell")

What we learned

Gene selection: the cause is found. The code version is not the cause (the public code did not change), and neither is the gene order (MI values are exactly the same whatever the order). Since our counts are the authors’ counts, our MI values are the authors’ too, and the difference lies only in the selection settings. The authors’ selection is reproduced exactly, in all three cell types, by one wrapper run per sender → receiver direction with:

  • 25 genes per run instead of the default max(15, min(4 × genes of interest, 100));
  • all the ligands or receptors of the direction as features of interest, not only the first 8;
  • the subtype metadata (labels) as a feature of interest on both sides (condition changes nothing).

The last 5 missing dendritic cell genes were the clue: they are the top genes of TMEM219 and TNFRSF14, the two receptors removed by the cap of 8. These settings are not those of the published wrapper, and the paper does not mention them: the authors probably changed the wrapper or called the selection function themselves.

Orientations: two effects. On the authors’ input without its 14 duplicated columns, which is exactly the input the settings above produce:

  • the links are unchanged (the same 525 gene–gene links, Jaccard index 1);
  • the orientation status of 17 % of the links changes (83 % agreement, none reversed), and the genuine causations change too (30 in both networks, but only 23 shared).

Between that input and our input of notebook 06 (default settings, about 7 % different genes), links differ more (Jaccard 0.82) but orientations agree on 94 % of shared links. So the duplicated columns mainly change the orientations, and the gene selection mainly changes the links. Figure 3 holds in the network without duplicates: the same distances for all the genes named in the paper, and CXCL12 → CFD is kept.

Summary: what changes what.

Change made to the input Effect on the links Effect on the orientations
Remove the 14 duplicated columns (same genes otherwise) none (same 525 links, Jaccard 1) 17 % of the links change status (none reversed); only 23 of the 30 genuine causations are shared
Default selection settings instead of the authors’ (about 7 % different genes) links differ more (Jaccard 0.82) 94 % of the shared links keep their orientation

The duplicated columns therefore act mainly on the orientations, and the gene selection mainly on the links.

What this means. Case study 2 can be rebuilt exactly from public data, provided the selection settings above are used. The duplicated columns are an artefact of the authors’ preparation: removing them changes no link but about one orientation in six, which confirms that MIIC’s orientations are much more sensitive to the input than its links.

What we did not test. We showed what removing the duplicates does to the authors’ input. We did not do the opposite experiment, which is the direct test of our hypothesis: adding the duplicated columns to the input we rebuild, and checking that MIIC then returns the authors’ network exactly. Logically it should: notebook 04 shows that MIIC on the authors’ input gives their network, and Part 1 shows that our selection gives their genes. But this is not verified, for two reasons. First, we cannot predict which 14 genes are duplicated (the naming rule of notebook 05 finds 11 of them but also 24 that the authors do not have), so the test would have to copy their 14 columns, which is partly circular. Second, we have not checked that the order of the columns, which does not change the MI values, has no effect on the orientations that MIIC finds.

We will not run it, because of the cost (about 3 hours of MIIC on one thread, the server’s settings), but it is the experiment to do to confirm the hypothesis:

  1. take our rebuilt input (authors’ settings: 25 genes per run, no cap of 8, labels as feature of interest);
  2. add the 14 duplicated columns, copied from the authors’ table, in the authors’ column order;
  3. run MIIC with the server’s settings (scripts/run_miic.R, one thread, same seed);
  4. compare with the authors’ network (links, orientations, genuine causations): if the duplicates are the only difference, the two networks should be identical.

Questions for the authors. How were the six wrapper runs pooled (origin of the duplicated columns)? Why 25 genes and no cap of 8, and are these the settings to use? Were the published L-R link strengths meant to come from a duplicated gene?
